data.title: Sanofi joins the peloton as '27 Tour de France partner
data.description:
Sanofi is gearing up for another major sports sponsorship in its home country, this time with the 2027 Tour de France.

The French pharma will be the first company to sponsor the prestigious white jersey, which recognizes the best rider under 25, at both the Tour de France and the women's Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift.

Sanofi will use the sponsorship and the races' massive global reach to “engage the public on health and science education” through initiatives developed in collaboration with patient organizations and healthcare professionals, it said in an Oct. 16 release. The programs will focus on prevention and patient support and take place throughout 2027 in stage towns, fan zones, along the race routes and online.

Between 10 million and 12 million spectators line the Tour de France route each year, providing a major audience alongside the estimated 150 million TV viewers the race reaches in Europe and broadcasts in 190 countries, according to Sanofi.

“The Tour de France has a unique ability to reach millions of people across France and around the world. We are harnessing this extraordinary reach in service of health,” Sanofi CEO Belén Garijo commented in the release. “Just like a cycling team in the peloton, where riders succeed by working together, we believe scientific progress is also a collective effort. Through the power of sport, we can connect with people, raise awareness of diseases and prevention, and make health information more accessible.”

In a one-minute video accompanying the announcement of Sanofi as a major partner of the race, the drugmaker further connects the cycling competition to “the race for better health," with a montage of fast-paced cyclists and cheering spectators interspersed with footage from Sanofi's labs.

“We’ll ride alongside the next generation of men and women who will compete for the white jersey and the future it represents,” a voiceover says, as the video shows a cyclist wearing the Sanofi-branded white jersey, complete with sleeve stripes and shorts in Sanofi's signature purple. “Like us, they know what it takes to keep going until they cross the finish line.”

The video calls the 2027 launch Sanofi's “largest health awareness campaign” and ends with a visualization of the race route outlined in Sanofi purple.

“Wherever the tour goes, we go,” the voiceover says. “The race for health is on.”

The partnership reflects both Sanofi's recent history of sponsoring major sporting events and its shared French roots with the Tour de France, bringing together “two institutions born in France and now recognized around the world,” Sanofi explained, noting that the two “share a commitment to excellence and endurance.”

By sponsoring both the women's and men's races, the company reflects a “coherent and inclusive vision of sport, excellence and visibility,” it added in an FAQ.

Through its recent sports partnerships, Sanofi has carved out a niche in “turning global reach into meaningful health impact,” as the company put it in the release.

In 2024, Sanofi launched what it called at the time the “biggest corporate activation” in its history during the Summer Olympics in Paris. The marketing push included digital activations throughout the event and its “Igniting Potential” campaign, which drew parallels between Sanofi scientists and Olympic athletes.

Last year, the company used the 24 Hours of Le Mans auto race to raise meningitis awareness by displaying the meningitis flag on two-time Le Mans winner United Autosports' No. 59 McLaren during the race, with the team's drivers also sporting the flag's colors.

More recently, Sanofi returned to the Olympic stage as an official health partner of the Special Olympics Unified Football World Cup in Paris. Also this year, the company sponsored Boston's involvement in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, with its head of external engagement, Tanisha Sullivan, joining an advisory board supporting the city's preparations for the tournament.

Elsewhere, Sanofi is using pickleball to encourage older adults to protect themselves against COVID-19 with its Nuvaxovid vaccine through a “Serve Up Protection” campaign with USA Pickleball. The company expanded its sports-related partnerships for Nuvaxovid with a new celebrity spokesperson, NBA champion Karl-Anthony Towns, who helped lead the New York Knicks to their first NBA title in 53 years this year.

data.title: Gilead kicks off Latino AIDS Awareness Day with new campaign
data.description:
With Oct. 15 marking National Latino AIDS Awareness Day, the time is “Ahorita Mismo" (Right Now!) to push for HIV prevention education in Hispanic and Latino communities, as Gilead Sciences expresses in its new campaign. 

The latest offshoot of Gilead's Care for the Culture initiative, the company's Ahora Mismo campaign targets Latino communities through trusted voices and culturally significant humor, a lane that's emerging as one right up Gilead’s alley. 

“While significant progress has been made in HIV prevention, gaps in awareness, stigma and access to information continue to impact many communities — including and especially Latino communities,” Gilead’s VP of marketing and U.S. prevention Ashley Gildea commented in an emailed statement. “Ahorita Mismo - meaning ‘right now’ - is a call to action rooted in the belief that timely information can help people make informed decisions about their health.”

"Through culturally grounded storytelling and community-centered engagement, this campaign seeks to elevate awareness of HIV testing and prevention options, spark meaningful conversations, and help ensure the Latino community has the information and support they need to take the next step toward protecting their health," Gildea said. 

The company’s minute-long “Ahorita Ghosted” spot, one of three that goes with the campaign, stars popular digital creators Eric Sedeño and Boman Martinez-Reid, the latter of whom will soon be seen in a Scottish castle in an upcoming season of Peacock’s hit reality show “The Traitors.” 

In the video, a retro display with a funky font and a catchy, Latin music-inspired background tune welcomes viewers to “1-800-Ahorita,” where “dating advance and HIV prevention get real” through fictional calls that speak to real-life situations. Sedeño and Martinez-Reid sit across each other in a comfy, realistic living room set under a neon “1-800-Ahorita” sign. After an unsuccessful round of rock paper scissors, the phone rings with their first caller, who shares the story of a man who “straight up ghosted” him. 

The potential reason for the ghost is soon revealed, and it’s not “accidentally liking one of his posts from 2019,” as Sedeño initially suggests. The man on the phone expresses that all he did was ask if his partner had been tested for HIV, a situation that Martinez-Reid maintains is “still salvageable.” Sedeño asks if the caller himself has been tested, which he was planning to “ahorita” (right now).

“Don’t ghost your sexual health,” Sedeño says in the video. “The impact of HIV continues to affect the Latino community.”

“A conversation with your healthcare provider about getting tested and learning your HIV prevention options can go a long way,” Martinez-Reid adds, to which Sedeño agrees. 

“Our health is something we should take care of ahorita mismo,” he says. The duo has successfully reassured the caller, leaving the two to end the ad with a jokey exchange and a silly montage of the friends posing in the living room set as a voiceover directs viewers to Gilead's Care for the Culture website. 

Related

Otters, bears and Pharma Lions: inside Gilead’s bronze-winning Cannes spot

Throughout the video, Sedeño and Martinez-Reid seamlessly slip in references familiar to the Latino community such as Sedeño calling the caller “corazón,” a common Spanish term of endearment. The digital creators repeat a similiar song and dance in "Ahorita Eggplant" and "Ahorita Throuple," in which they encourage other callers who reach out with sticky dating situations to meet with a healthcare provider to discuss their HIV status. 

Black and Hispanic communities both experience a greater HIV burden, according to Gilead and Emory University’s AIDSVu. In 2024, Hispanic/Latino individuals represented 34% of all new HIV diagnoses in the U.S., despite making up only 19% of the population, and had an HIV prevalence rate that was more than three times higher than for white individuals. 

Care for the Culture looks to emphasize the importance of HIV prevention across these communities, reminding its audience that “HIV is not somewhere else. It’s right here,” the website says, noting that seven out of every ten estimated new HIV infections occurred within Black and Latino communities as of 2022.

In Care for the Culture’s efforts to strike up conversations around HIV and destigmatize testing and prevention, Gilead previously used the power of music and renowned R&B singer TLC’s Tionne “T-Boz” Watkins in “So We PrEP,” a remix of TLC’s 1994 hit “Creep.”  

More recently, Gilead has looked to reach Black communities through other Care for the Culture initiatives such as its “Up to Date” campaign, which saw comedian and podcast host Nicole Byers using culturally relevant language and humor to spread HIV education in a spot that also included “Saturday Night Live” alum Devon Walker. 

Both “Up to Date” and “Ahorita” include storylines and verbiage that are relatable to modern dating and sexual culture, such as the late-night hook-up depicted in “Up to Date” or the ghosting conundrum in “Ahorita.” The topical tropes speak to Gilead’s evolving messaging around HIV as the company moves beyond scientific-focused content to centering “authenticity” and directness, executive director of public affairs, U.S. advocacy and health equity Deborah Wafer explained in a July interview with Fierce. 

“We need to be more direct and talk about sex and talk about prevention of HIV,” Wafer said, with one way to do so being through “the right language” that younger generations can pick up on. 

As the maker of the first-ever pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) option back in 2012, Gilead has been at the forefront of HIV prevention and, in turn, HIV drug marketing since the beginning. The company’s collection of HIV products includes top-selling treatment Biktarvy, daily PrEP Descovy and most recently long-acting PrEP injection Yeztugo. In 2025, Gilead picked up $20.8 billion in HIV-specific sales, a 6% jump from 2024.

data.title: Compass puts resistant depression on the map with awareness day
data.description:
Compass Pathways has partnered with mental health organizations on the first-ever awareness day for treatment-resistant depression (TRD). 

The biotech, which is developing a drug candidate based on the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, is working on the awareness day with the National Alliance on Mental Illness, Mental Health America and the Depression and Bipolar Support Alliance (DBSA). The mental health organizations are sharing information and resources about TRD. 

Compass quoted data showing that TRD affects an estimated 4 million people in the U.S., of whom fewer than 5% are on a treatment indicated for the form of depression. Johnson & Johnson’s Spravato became the first monotherapy approved for adults with TRD in the U.S. in January 2025. 

J&J has worked to raise awareness of depression, including by launching its “Generation Fine” campaign in May. However, physicians continue to see gaps in awareness of TRD, as Sagar Parikh, M.D., vice chair of DBSA’s scientific advisory board, explained in a statement. 

“When depression continues despite multiple treatment attempts, many people do not realize they may be experiencing TRD,” Parikh said. “TRD Awareness Day can help both patients and clinicians better understand that this is a distinct condition, separate from major depressive disorder, and recognize when it may be time to ask different questions about care strategies.”

Aiming to launch its TRD drug in the first half of 2027, Compass is preparing for commercialization. Last month, the biotech launched “Change the Tune in TRD,” an education campaign focused on U.S. healthcare providers. Compass is running the campaign to provide evidence-based education on the longer, more persistent episodes associated with TRD. 

Alongside the awareness day unveiling, the company shared details of its efforts to understand the lives of people with TRD. A Compass survey found nearly 95% of TRD patients describe themselves as either functioning but struggling, surviving day to day or barely getting by. 

The impacts extend beyond patients with TRD. Almost two in three caregivers say TRD impacts the whole family’s social, physical or mental health. More than half of people say that caregiving has taken a major toll on their mental health. Compass plans to share the full survey report in the future.

data.title: Sanofi dodges fine over alleged disparagement of CSL flu vaccine
data.description:
Sanofi has avoided a European Union fine after antitrust regulators accepted its commitments to address the alleged disparagement of CSL Seqirus’ rival flu vaccine.

The European Commission opened an antitrust investigation in June to assess whether Sanofi’s alleged disparagement campaign against CSL’s Fluad violated EU competition rules. Sanofi proposed pledges to resolve the case, leading the Commission to assess the impact of the company’s commitments in July and August. 

The Commission accepted Sanofi’s commitments Wednesday, sparing the company from antitrust fines it can impose for disparaging rivals. Teresa Ribera, the EU’s executive vice president for clean, just and competitive transition, explained the decision at a press conference.

Sanofi immediately approached the Commission “in a cooperative mood,” Ribera said. The company’s engagement enabled the Commission to quickly identify the remedies to ensure “a prompt reaction and a prompt enforcement of the law,” she said, adding that the resolution was “good, sufficient and immediate,” the official added. 

Ribera pushed back on a reporter’s suggestion that sparing Sanofi from a fine would encourage other companies to disparage their rivals. The speed with which Sanofi reacted to the investigation showed that “they are absolutely convinced of our capacity to be tough on this,” she said. Ribera expects Sanofi to comply with the commitments, but her team “will remain vigilant on what they are doing.”

Legally binding commitments prohibit Sanofi from making certain statements in promotional materials aimed at healthcare professionals in Germany and France. Until March 2030, Sanofi cannot criticize, cast doubt upon or contradict national vaccination recommendations or highlight Fluad negatively, or unduly suggest that its own vaccine, Efluelda, is safer or more effective. 

For two years, Sanofi’s German and French websites must acknowledge that the applicable national vaccination recommendations treat Fluad and Efluelda as equivalent in protecting elderly people against the flu, both having a robust evidence base. Sanofi must send the statement to healthcare professionals and key opinion leaders in Germany who previously received the allegedly disparaging materials.

data.title: AbbVie slots in ‘Time For Treks’ with CLL community walk
data.description:
AbbVie, the National Park Foundation (NPF) and CLL Society are working together to immerse people with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) in the beauty of community and the great outdoors with a new “Time For Treks” campaign. 

Kicking off Oct. 17, the organizations will host a free blood cancer community walk at Cabrillo National Monument in San Diego, California. The event is welcome to people with CLL, caregivers and supporters and focuses on fostering outdoor experiences and connections within the community. 

“Because every person's experience with CLL is different, every trek can look different, too,” CLL Society reminded potential trekkers on its LinkedIn page, encouraging visitors to “choose the route and pace that feels right for you.” 

The campaign stems from AbbVie’s deep understanding of the CLL patient community, “not just as patients, but as people,” senior director of patient advocacy, oncology portfolio Christine Armstrong explained in an interview with Fierce. According to Armstrong, one activity that has come up “time and time again” in discussions with patients is a love of the outdoors and hiking with friends and family. 

“Time For Treks” naturally came to life when the company pondered how it can continue to “really meet patients where they are,” Armstrong said. The initiative’s name signifies the moments during a patient’s treatment journey where they get a chance to step away and perhaps engage in a nature-based activity. 

“The campaign itself, it was really co-created with patients,” Armstrong said. 

One patient whose insights helped form the program is Alejandro, an environmental engineer with CLL who was featured in AbbVie’s 2025 short film “Second Winds.” The documentary saw CLL patients Alejandro, Christina and Jeff sharing their individual stories and staying active through activities such as hiking, biking and more. Alejandro’s input was “reminiscent of many other patients’ insights about loving to be outdoors,” Armstrong noted. 

Related

AbbVie short film showcases 'Second Winds' of life after CLL diagnosis

AbbVie and the National Park Foundation have plans to expand the initiative to other national parks in the future, as both align on a mission to “encourage people to get out” and plan treks within their own communities or local parks. 

Between the joint priorities of the National Park Foundation, AbbVie, the CLL society and the patient community, “I think that this is that kind of perfect synergized campaign,” Armstrong said. 

At the launch on Oct. 17, AbbVie will leverage its educational website on navigating and managing CLL, which contains information on treatment options and approaches as well as other tips and resources for living with CLL. 

AbbVie has been supporting CLL patients through its Johnson & Johnson-partnered BTK inhibitor Imbruvica since its initial 2013 approval and its Genentech-partnered BCL-2 inhibitor Venclexta, which first hit the market in 2016. 

In 2024, the company dug into the emotional experience of a CLL diagnoses with a survey that was the first to break down the results by race/ethnicity to highlight the differing mental health impacts and desired support resources.

data.title: UCB fashions ‘Wear It Out’ project with empowering t-shirts
data.description:
UCB is encouraging people with immunology-driven diseases such as hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis (PsA) to wear their heart on their sleeve in a new community-driven program.  

For those living with chronic skin conditions such as psoriasis, HS and PsA, deciding what to wear each day can be a battle that goes beyond style. Those with plaque psoriasis may avoid black clothing due to fear of visible skin flaking on the fabric, while people with HS might worry about drainage or leaking from a disease flare showing up on white clothing. 

Patients with stiff or painful joints from PsA, meanwhile, may struggle with the act of getting dressed itself, especially when dealing with things such as buttons on clothes, UCB explained in a release. 

Now, the disease community can reclaim white and black t-shirts with “Wear It Out,” hallmarked by a one-of-a-kind, “condition-conscious” t-shirt line made by graphic artist Sophia Yeshi. Yeshi worked with patients and advocates to create designs that “reflects the beauty, courage and individuality of the community,” Yeshi noted. 

“My work explores themes of identity, resilience, and belonging, so when I was given the opportunity to create something beautiful out of the often challenging experiences of real people living with these conditions, I was so inspired,” Yeshi said in the release. "Every person who shared their story brought a unique perspective and sense of strength to this project.”

Printed on a custom blend of bamboo and organic cotton specifically meant to be a skin-safe, non-irritating blend for patients with the skin diseases, the t-shirts come in white and black and depict a colorful display of self-expression, featuring abstract people surrounded by a wave of blue, orange and purple hues. On the black and white t-shirts, the designs become “symbols of the choices others may never understand,” UCB said. 

Related

UCB partners with Dr. Pimple Popper in ongoing hidradenitis suppurativa campaign

“Getting dressed should not be a strategic decision, and feeling comfortable in your own body should never feel out of reach, but for many people with HS, PSO, or PsA, it can be [by] quietly ruling out a white or black shirt or skipping an invitation because of what the condition may show,” UCB’s head of patient strategy, U.S. immunology Brittany Blair explained. 

“Wear It Out transforms that quiet calculation into a visual community symbol worth celebrating and it is a reminder that no one should have to settle for less than feeling like themselves in their healthcare journey.”

“Wear It Out” shines a light on the unseen disease impacts of the approximately 2.5 million people living with HS in the U.S. and the some 11.3 million with psoriasis or PsA.  To get in on the wearable t-shirt aspect of the project, patients are encouraged to visit the associated campaign website to join the “Wear It Out” community, engage with educational and treatment resources and share their own story via audio or video to receive their own shirt. 

Patients must share their story to receive a shirt, but contributions don’t have to be lengthy and won’t be used by UCB without consent, the company emphasizes on the website. 

“Whether it’s just a thought or a more detailed experience, every story helps bring the Wear It Out program to life,” the website explains.

An “explore treatment” tab on the site directs patients to UCB’s product website for Bimzelx, the company’s FDA-approved biologic for psoriasis, PsA, non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and HS. 

Last month, Bimzelx took the top spot on iSpot.TV’s monthly ranking of drug ad spending, reflecting both streaming data and traditional linear TV. According to iSpot, UCB spent a total of $56.9 million on Bimzelx streaming and linear ads in September as the company looks to further expand the reach of its immunology blockbuster.

data.title: Galderma sculpts new narrative around menopausal skin changes
data.description:
One in two women is unaware that hormonal fluctuations during perimenopause and menopause can affect their skin, a Galderma survey found.

Galderma, a dermatology specialist, recently worked with Perspectus Global to survey 5,090 women who have experienced or are experiencing perimenopause or menopause in the U.K., the U.S., Brazil and China. More than half of the respondents initially attributed menopause-related skin changes to general aging. Fewer than one-third of the women recognized the link to menopause.

The misconceptions affected skin care purchases, with 70% buying products designed to address signs of aging in response to skin changes during perimenopause or menopause. Almost half of the respondents struggled to find information, in part because advice focuses on aging over menopause. 

Galderma is working to fill the perceived advice gap ahead of World Menopause Day on Oct. 18. Framing its research as evidence of “The Menopausal Skin Misread,” the company has launched a campaign to share scientific evidence and women’s stories. The “Rewriting the Future of Your Skin, Own your Menopause Story” campaign includes a website that explains how hormonal changes affect the skin.

The survey points to demand for such information. More than 80% of respondents agreed that they would feel more informed and in control of their skin care decisions if they better understood the differences between general aging and menopause-related skin changes.

Galderma is launching the awareness drive following research into the effects of its Restylane Skinboosters and Sculptra products on menopausal women. The study, which Galderma supported, linked the use of Restylane Skinboosters followed by Sculptra to increased facial dermal thickness.

Sculptra, an injectable cosmetic, is a key product for Galderma. Double-digit Sculptra growth in the U.S. and international markets helped (PDF) Galderma’s filler and biostimulator sales rise 10.5% to $611 million in the second quarter. Galderma named geographic expansion of Sculptra sales as one of its five key opportunities for the rest of the year.

data.title: Invenra joins the ADC game with custom card deck
data.description:
Invenra has created playing cards featuring artwork by people affected by cancer as it seeks biopharma buy-in for its antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) service. 

The Wisconsin-based antibody service provider has started using its bispecific and trispecific antibody platforms to generate ADC targeting moieties. To support the rollout, Invenra has arrived at the World ADC Conference in San Diego with its “52 Views of Cancer” playing card deck. Each of the 52 cards, plus the jokers and box cover, features art that Invenra has licensed from people affected by cancer. 

Invenra CEO Roland Green came up with the idea for the deck while looking at artwork by his daughter, who was recently diagnosed with ovarian cancer. Viewing the artwork, Green envisioned “a collection of art that highlights the patients’ stories, with a goal of inspiring the scientists and clinicians in their effort to find cures,” the CEO said in a statement.

The “52 Views of Cancer” website displays each artwork and statements from the artists. The deck has a wide array of art styles, with the aces alone featuring a digital collage, an oil painting and a watercolor and ink piece. Their stories are similarly varied, reflecting the impact cancer has on patients and their loved ones.

Invenra’s deployment of the cards at the World ADC Conference is the start of an ongoing effort. The company plans to share the decks at other conferences to expose researchers, clinicians and scientists to patients’ voices and perspectives.

The deck adds to the long history of using playing cards for awareness and marketing. Bayer created a deck in the 1960s. Roche followed suit around 1980. More recently, Amylyx Pharmaceuticals used a playing card design to make its disease education website simpler and more approachable. And Maat Pharma created a version of the game “happy families” to educate people about the gut microbiota.

data.title: UCB’s Bimzelx takes the drug ad spending top spot
data.description:
UCB’s immunology drug Bimzelx has once again become the highest ranked drug in iSpot.TV’s pharma ad spending league as it topped the charts for September. 

The Belgian pharma’s med took no. 1 position as iSpot.TV has, as of September, started adding streaming data—as well as traditional linear TV—to its monthly analysis. 

This is because streaming is increasingly important to drug marketers—and thus for drugmakers’ wallets. UCB spent a total of $56.9 million in Bimzelx ads last month, with that split across 53.85% for streaming and 46.15% in linear. 

UCB also took the spot with its immunology therapy in August, although this only counted linear TV promotion, where the company spent $31.2 million at the time. 

Eli Lilly’s recently launched obesity drug Foundayo saw a major jump in September, too, where it has not typically been troubling the top 10, coming in second place. The pharma giant spent $52.5 million on the drug in total, but this was heavily skewed (63.05% of spend) to streaming compared to Lilly's outlay of 36.95% on linear. 

Related

UCB’s Bimzelx comes from out of the blue to claim August’s top pharma ad spending spot

A familiar face in AbbVie’s immunology therapy Skyrizi came in third position, with the company spending $44.7 million altogether. This was, unlike the top two, split in favor of traditional TV ads, with 33.84% spent on streaming and 66.16% linear. 

It was a similar story for AbbVie's second immunology drug Rinvoq, coming in fourth place, with a $40.7 million spending total split 31.91% on streaming and 68.09% on linear.

In fifth and down two spots was Johnson & Johnson’s immunology drug Tremfya, which in the first half of the year had been vying with Skyrizi as the drug with the highest ad spend. 

Spend on Tremfya was only around $400,000 less than Rinvoq for the period, though the majority of this (73.75%) was spent on linear ads. 

Novo’s obesity drug Wegovy jumped back into the top 10 in September in sixth place, while Johnson & Johnson’s atypical antipsychotic drug Caplyta fell two spots to seventh. 

J&J also saw its new oral moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis drug Icotyde fall two spots down to eighth place with $33.1 million total in spend.

Eli Lilly’s injectable obesity drug Zepbound, not in the top 10 in August, rose up to ninth last month with 81.71% of its total spend of $24.3 million earmarked for linear ads. 

In tenth place, as it was in August, was AbbVie’s neurology drug Vraylar, with $22.3 million spend across streaming and linear.

data.title: Arcutis springs new Zoryve awareness campaign with Simone Biles
data.description:
Arcutis Biotherapeutics has lined up another celeb to tout the benefits of its topical skin medicine Zoryve, adding world-renowned gymnast Simone Biles to its all-star team of spokespeople. 

The company’s “Skin to Believe In” awareness campaign featuring Biles targets the approximately 36 million people in the U.S. who live with inflammatory skin conditions such as seborrheic dermatitis and atopic dermatitis, the most common form of eczema. 

Biles herself spent “years” trying different over-the-counter products to calm her itchy, flaking scalp and dry patches on her arms before getting diagnoses from a dermatologist and finding a steroid-free option that works for her in Zoryve, according to Arcutis. Today, the athlete uses Zoryve in its foam formulation for her seb derm and the cream version for her eczema. 

“I like Zoryve because it is not a steroid, pill, injection, or shampoo and it's easy to use, not greasy, and fits into my routine,” Biles said in a company release. “Using Zoryve reduced the flakes and itching on my scalp, which bothered me the most, and the eczema spots on my arms are also clearer, too.”

Through “Skin to Believe In,” Biles encourages others who may have the inflammatory skin conditions to bring up the topic with a healthcare provider and seek treatment options. 

“I’ve learned that we can’t fix every problem on our own and it’s OK to seek help,” continued Biles. “I believe how you care for yourself reflects how you carry yourself, and by partnering with Arcutis on this awareness campaign I believe we can break the stigma associated with chronic skin conditions by helping people feel empowered to speak with a healthcare provider about their symptoms so that they can find a treatment that works for them.”

According to Arcutis CEO Frank Watanabe, Biles’ first encounter with Zoryve came organically and started on social media. The gymnast opened up about her experience with seborrheic dermatitis and eczema symptoms in a TikTok post around the time of the Paris 2024 Summer Olympics, he explained in an interview. Upon bringing up her itchy, flaky scalp on her large social media platform, dermatologists recognized the seb derm symptoms and encouraged her to check out some of the FDA-approved products available for the condition, which is how she ultimately got started on Zoryve and connected with Arcutis. 

“She’s a very enthusiastic supporter of the product,” Watanabe said. “Working with her is great.” 

Biles isn’t the only Zoryve spokesperson who organically came across the product. So did professional golfer Max Homa and the mother-daughter duo of actress Tori Spelling and her teenage daughter, Stella McDermott. All three are a part of Arcutis’ recent “Free to Be Me” awareness campaign, which looked to bring attention to the skin conditions and help people who may suffer from them recognize the symptoms.  

People with inflammatory skin conditions often don’t realize that they have a treatable medical condition, Watanabe explained, living with symptoms such as itching, sleep disruptions or depression and navigating stigma that can be attached to the visible symptoms of the conditions. Finding a treatment that’s approved for continuous use like Zoryve can be a “real game changer for patients,” the CEO said. 

Related

Arcutis' Zoryve bags 2nd FDA nod, this time as a foam to treat 'the great neglected disease in dermatology'

Amongst its peers in the non-steroid, topical dermatitis crowd, Zoryve is the only product that’s also approved in a foam formulation, which can better reach hard-to-treat areas such as the scalp. So far since its 2023 launch, Zoryve foam already makes up over half of the drug’s total sales, pulling down $67.4 million over the second quarter of 2026 compared to the $62.4 million across Zoryve cream’s various dose strengths. 

“It’s a really unique product,” Watanabe said of Zoryve foam, adding that it “just fits in with patients’ lives.” 

Next year, fast-growing Zoryve could snag another label expansion to cover infants aged three to 24 months with atopic dermatitis, which would be its eighth nod since its initial 2022 approval. This one would cover an area Watanabe knows well; his own son had eczema when he was a baby, meaning he can personally speak to the inconvenience of applying twice-daily topical steroids to young children. Zoryve, meanwhile, has a once-daily application and is already garnering buzz across pediatric dermatologists, who currently “just don’t have good options for these kids,” the CEO said. 

Still, there remains work to be done to grow the addressable patient population as more than half of people with psoriasis, seb derm or eczema aren’t currently seeking treatment, Watanabe noted. To help make treatment options available to people who may not have access to local dermatologists, Arcutis this summer launched a virtual health platform that quickly connects patients with independent dermatologists. 

“We’re helping to make specialized dermatology care a lot more accessible to patients, no matter where that patient is,” Watanabe explained. 

Outside of its awareness campaigns, Zoryve has also been building a name for itself outside of the strictly medical field. This month, Marie Claire magazine bestowed Zoryve cream with its 2026 Best Prescription Skin Solution Award, adding to a stack of similar honors from Allure and Glamour magazine. 

Watanabe attributes Zoryve’s unique recognition in the beauty space to “the thoughtful way that we formulated these products” and notes that the skin market itself is a “very patient-driven sector” that’s subject to a different level of patient engagement due to the visibility of the disease and its response to treatment. Given that, awareness campaigns and recognized spokespeople like Biles can “really help motivate people to seek treatment.”

“When you see someone like Simone, who's so relatable and so I think well-liked and respected, talking about her own condition and what she went through, the struggle she went through, and how going to see a dermatology clinician and getting on prescription treatment has really changed her life for the better. I think it helps people demystify it, destigmatize it,” Watanabe said.
